utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we continue with the first Defence witness, the Trial Chamber wishes to inform the parties about two decisions. Yesterday, after the opening statement of the Defence, two procedural issues were raised by the Prosecution: First, the question of the alibi by Defence; second, the question whether the second Defence witness, Witness M, is a trial witness or an expert witness. With regard to these issues, the Trial Chamber rules as follows: First, after having heard the argument of the parties and after further consultations, the Chamber is of the opinion that the Defence argument that Mr. Naletilic was in a house together with some children at the time ^ outside the salvic -- sounds like in question does constitute an alibi defence. Pursuant to Rule 67(A)(ii)(a), the Defence should have notified the Prosecutor of their intent to offer this Defence of alibi prior to the commencement of the trial. However, Article 67(b) clearly states that failure of the Defence to provide notice under this Rule shall not limit the right of the accused to testify on alibi defence. The Trial Chamber therefore orders the Defence to provide specific information to the Prosecution pursuant to Rule 67(A)(ii)(a) at this stage of the proceedings about the place and the accused -- about the place the accused claimed to have been present at the time of the alleged crime, the names and addresses of the witnesses, and any other evidence upon which the accused intends to rely to establish the alibi. Secondly, regarding the witness status of Defence Witness M, the Trial Chamber yesterday heard arguments of the parties. The Defence argued that the witness will testify about his personal experience and not appear as a general expert. The Chamber is of the view that this argument is supported by the witness summaries provided by Defence in all pre-Defence filings. The Chamber therefore shared the opinion of the Defence that Witness M will testify as a trial witness. With regard to the Prosecution's application to receive a statement of the witness from other proceedings, the Chamber would like to ask the Defence to indicate whether it's possible to rearrange Witness M to testify at a later stage, maybe as the third or fourth witness of the Defence. This rearrangement would give some time to wait for the decision on the variance of the confidentiality of the statement, which would be fair to the Prosecution. Yesterday, the Chamber had the impression the Defence is generally not opposed to such a solution. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as Witness M is concerned, in any event, we wanted to suggest to Your Honours -- because this is something I mentioned yesterday, that the Defence had understanding for this, because when it was preparing its cross-examinations, it had to go through this too. However, Your Honour, the Prosecution is a single organisation, it has unified services, and having obtained the names from the Defence in time, given that Witness M was an expert, they could have obtained an expertise, an expert report from their service. But the Defence is afraid that we won't even have time to start with the witness this week, or that if we do start with this witness, we won't have the time for cross-examination. So we were going to suggest -- I had the intention of speaking to my learned colleagues today about this and to suggest to them that if we started with this, we should finish the examination-in-chief, and then, after the holidays, to have my colleagues conduct the cross-examination. I think that this would be fair. The witness is here. It would be a pity to lose him now. I think the next one is arriving today or tomorrow. If we finish with the first witness, we could start with the second witness, so we could conclude this, because I know that we only have tomorrow left to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I appreciate very much your efforts towards this direction, but you have to be realistic. In your summaries, you said that the first witness will take us five hours for you to directly examine him. Yesterday we only spent about one hour, and today is three hours, more or less. And there will be the cross-examination. That will take today and most part of tomorrow. So my suggestion is that for this week we won't hear any more witnesses at all, because we could not afford to have a witness under the oath for a very long weekend spent in Mostar. So we'll start the next -- the second witness next week, and whenever we finish the first witness, we will rise for this week. Is that agreeable?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I was afraid of suggesting this, since we're always attempting to do as much work as possible, but I agree with this absolutely and I support your proposal absolutely. If the Tribunal considers that we should postpone this even more, we'll have witnesses for after the holidays, and then Witness 3 would become Witness 2. We can do this, too. That's absolutely no problem. It's no problem to make such a change either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. I think that what Your Honour has proposed this morning is acceptable. It's fine to the Prosecution side. I think that if Witness 2 begins testifying next week, we will be prepared to proceed with cross-examination of that witness, provided that in the meantime we've been able to get the expert report from the other case unsealed. This is obviously not something that the Defence has a position on or that they can -- I'm not suggesting that the Defence can do anything to speed that process up. We are attempting to do what needs to be done, including filing an amended, if you will, application this morning with that Appeals Chamber to get the matter before the Appeals Chamber. Hopefully, the Defence attorneys in the other case will not object to the unsealing of that report, and if that takes place, then we should be prepared to proceed, again, provided that the testimony is as a precipient witness in that Witness 2 does not end up testifying as an expert. But based on the assurances given by counsel, we're confident that's not going to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Should we go to the closed session and call the first witness? Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go to the closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, before the witness comes in, I have an announcement to make. This afternoon, we'll have the ex parte hearing in the Courtroom I - in Courtroom I - thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Please remember that you're still under the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, yesterday the last question was about what do you know -- what happened on the 6th of May in the Polog village near Mostar. I think that was the last question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the 6th of May, 1991, in the presidency, on the 5th in the evening, we were discussing a matter in the presidency. We were discussing about what to do with regard to that event because we knew that the tank brigade had left Mostar and it was passing through Siroki Brijeg in the direction of Kupres. For us in the presidency, we knew that that tank brigade wasn't going to be involved in military manoeuvres because they were present in Mostar -- they had been present in Mostar for over 40 years and around Mostar they had training grounds for training. They went there with another intention, and the population in the surroundings of Mostar, and especially in Siroki Brijeg, was quite aware of this fact. And the population, the inhabitants in that area, prevented in a civilised and dignified manner -- without it involving an armed conflict, they tried to persuade them in a democratic and civilised way; they tried to persuade them to turn back, to turn back to where they had come from. However, as I -- as far as I can remember, that lasted for two or three days, this attempt for the civilian population and the command to outwit each other, the command of this tank brigade. And even the Supreme Commander, that is to say, General Kadijevic, who was in charge of national defence, he called two or three times. He called Alija Izetbegovic two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. Could you tell this Tribunal who General Kadijevic is and who the Secretary for National Defence is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Kadijevic was the Federal Secretary for National Defence in Belgrade, and he was also the commander of all the armed services in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the territory of Yugoslavia as a whole. He called Alija Izetbegovic to tell him that someone from the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina should go into the field -- should go to the field and should remove, as he called them, the mob, the civilians, because otherwise if this was not done, they would be killed. So we in the presidency had a meeting, and we discussed what we should do and we discussed who should go there and what should be told -- what we should tell the population. It was logical for the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic -- it was logical for him to go and for me to go with Mr. Izetbegovic since I was from that area and I had been elected by the population on the whole. I had been elected to the presidency. But the other members didn't agree with this, but a decision was taken to go to that location, and Alija Izetbegovic was to go there with Mr. Kljuic, who was a reserve captain in the Yugoslav People's Army. And as such, in that capacity, there were relations between the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Yugoslav People's Army. I should also emphasise, draw your attention to why they didn't include me in the delegation. That was because in that presidency, at that meeting of the presidency, I said that I would tell the truth, I would tell the people the truth, and that they should then draw their own conclusions as to what they should do. And the truth was that -- and this is something that would be revealed later. The truth was that they weren't going to Kupres to train but it was part of a so-called military -- military move, and that move wanted to create a greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You mentioned the military plan RAM. Could you explain to us very briefly, please -- I'm letting you talk quite freely, but could you be a little more concise and a little more rapid, if possible.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military RAM, R-A-M, as far as I know, included all the key positions so that the Yugoslav People's Army as far as Bosnia-Herzegovina is concerned -- all the key positions that the Yugoslav People's Army should take. And these were Mostar, Kupres, Makljan, near Gornji Vakuf, and Bosanski Brod. And in Croatia, it was to take all the positions from Virovitica to Karlobag -- all the areas from Virovitica to Karlobag. This was in fact a plan developed by the Academy of Serbian Science, a plan for the creation of a greater Serbia, instead of the already defunct Yugoslavia. So they went to Siroki Brijeg, that is to say to Polog. And Alija Izetbegovic tried to persuade those people that he wasn't deceiving them, that that tank brigade was really going to Kupres because they wanted to train there and so on. And the people there, once again they believed Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. However, that tank brigade stayed in Kupres for a short period of time. They headed towards Glamoc. And during that time, they made secret routes from Glamoc to Kupres. And some tanks in Kupres or a little outside of Kupres covered with hay -- were covered with hay so that when they were needed in combat when fighting the HVO, in such a case they would be able to launch a surprise attack. And this is what they did. Before the attack itself in Kupres, around the 1st of April, 1992, given the incidents there, in the Presidency in Sarajevo we decided that we should go to Kupres and that Biljana Plavsic and I should go to Kupres in order to try and calm the situation down and prevent the worst from happening. We met with the local representatives of the Serbian Democratic Party there and of the Croatian Democratic Union. We had some meetings, and we discussed the matter. My suggestion was that together with the local heads of the Croatian Democratic Union -- my suggestion was that they should come to an agreement with the local Serbia people, that they could do this, but without the influence of the Yugoslav army and certain other foreigners of Serbia origin who had come to Kupres in order to disturb the relations between the Croatian and the Serbia people. And we almost managed to agree on this for the local population, the Serbian and Croatian population. We almost managed to agree on them finding a solution, a common solution, and to avoid any incidents. However, towards the very end, we were almost afraid that we had reached an agreement. At that point, the Serbian side went to a meeting. And it had been summoned by the local command of the Yugoslav People's Army. After 10 or 15 minutes, they returned -- the Serbian representatives returned to talks, and they told us that the Yugoslav People's Army did not agree, that they should withdraw from Kupres. But they considered themselves to be foreigners, foreigners in Kupres, and they were the ones who didn't allow the local population, the local Croat and Serbian population to come to an agreement. Those negotiations fell through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you tell us, do you know whether they really attacked Kupres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that evening - it was quite late - those talks were ongoing. Biljana Plavsic returned again through those areas which were under the control of the Yugoslav People's Army. She returned to Sarajevo. I wanted to go to Mostar, but I stayed on in Tomislavgrad in that night. In that evening, I went to talk with local representatives of the Croatian people, especially with representatives of the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union, and at that point they told me that something was being prepared, some major evil. I asked them when they expected this to happen, and they said, "Perhaps even this evening." In fact, I remained in a modest hotel, and about two or three hours later, I heard the sound of cannons firing, guns firing, mortars. I heard the sirens of ambulances. Later on, while at breakfast, the chief of the municipality, a Croat, he came to visit me. We had breakfast together and he told me that a conflict had broken out, a large-scale conflict, and that the Croatian side had suffered serious losses because they had been surprised by those tanks which had been covered with hay. They had been covered with hay. And this lasted for about a year, I think, with those tanks that had been concealed. And there was a lot of fog, of course, so that the HVO soldiers weren't able to find their bearings. And there were a lot of victims on the Croatian side. Many men were captured. On that day, I carried on. I continued to Mostar. I wanted to return from Mostar and go to Sarajevo through Jablanica, via Jablanica and Konjic, but at the exit from Mostar towards Sarajevo, I was prevented from doing so. There were Serbian barricades there. So I had to take a mountain route through Rakitna and Blidinja up in Jablanica. I had to return to Sarajevo via a very difficult route.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Witness, if you know, what the position and reaction was in September 1992 with respect to the village of Ravno.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of September, or rather, up to the end of September, that is to say, throughout September 1991, there were vast military forces moving from Serbia and Montenegro, well equipped. They were the military forces of the Yugoslav People's Army and they were on the move, as were various Serb paramilitary units. And these were joined by local Serb armed people, local armed Serbs, groups, little ones, bigger ones. At the time in the presidency, we assumed that in the course of September alone, over 100.000 soldiers, who were well armed, well equipped with modern weaponry, that they had crossed over into Bosnia-Herzegovina, and let's say half of these, so that would be about 50.000 soldiers, with the paramilitary forces, went towards Croatia and the Krajina area, and the other 50.000 soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army remained in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Roughly half/half in Northern Bosnia, or rather, Bosanska Posavina - and around 20.000 of those soldiers, Serbs and Montenegrins, reservists with military equipment, came and stayed in Mostar and its environs - and Eastern Herzegovina, down towards Trebinje, Popovo Polje, which is where the village of Ravno lies. The first conflict which took place, we can say that it was a war conflict, occurred in that village of Ravno, and it was predominantly a Croatian village. Most of the inhabitants were Croats. The village was burnt down, the people were killed. Some of them were taken prisoner. A very small number managed to escape. We talked to the Yugoslav People's Army and we said that a member of the presidency should go and see what had happened there, and we decided that Mr. Ejub Ganic would be the best person, as a member of the presidency, that he should go and see for himself, and the charge d'affaires of the President of the Croatian Democratic Union, Miljenko Brkic, was to accompany him. The two of them went to that area. However, the Yugoslav People's Army did not allow them to enter the village. They were only allowed to view it from a distance, from a nearby hill, and to look down on the village from that vantage point. So visually they were able to conclude that the village had in fact been destroyed, burnt. There was still smoke coming out of some of the houses and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what the reaction was, you as the presidency. Did you go to Belgrade for any negotiations? What was Alija Izetbegovic's reaction, the SDA party? Can you tell us something about that? Did Mr. Alija Izetbegovic make any statements in that regard? What was his attitude and conduct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Mr. Ejub Ganic returned to the presidency, he informed them of what he had actually seen down there, and he told us that the Yugoslav People's Army did not allow them to enter the village personally and to look at the situation in greater detail, to take stock of it in greater detail. I insisted that we protest, that we go to the Yugoslav army and protest, and say that we, as the presidency, would like something -- some steps to be taken. We wanted to take steps to prevent anything similar happening in the future in Bosnia-Herzegovina, at least in that portion of it which was still not under Serb control. We know that up until then, the Serb side had already taken over almost 70 per cent - together, of course, with the Yugoslav People's Army - of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It did not control the area of Herzegovina. That was the only area where the inhabitants were predominantly Croats, and they had organised themselves and set up resistance. And the other area was Bosanska Posavina and certain parts of Central Bosnia, especially the Lasva River Valley from Kilseljak to Travnik. They hadn't reached that part yet. The units of Yugoslav People's Army or Serbian paramilitary units hadn't succeeded in carrying out what they had carried out in the village of Ravno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you happen to go to Belgrade yourself perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After all these occurrences, we discussed what should be done in the presidency. The presidency discussed what we should do, in view of the fact that the Yugoslav People's Army was passing through Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Serb forces. They were doing what they wanted. They didn't ask us. They didn't ask the presidency for permission whether they could pass through, stay on, et cetera. And then the presidency, one afternoon, decided to send a presidency delegation urgently to Belgrade for talks with this General, General Kadijevic, who was the Federal Secretary for National defence at the time. The conclusion was the following: We were to request of the Federal Secretary for National Defence that all military units which had crossed over the border of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Serbia and Montenegro should return and take the same route back home. Of course, those forces who were still in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the ones that had already left and crossed Bosnian territory to enter Croatia, of course we couldn't ask them to return. And we also asked that in future, nobody from the Serbian and Montenegrin side would be allowed to enter Bosnia-Herzegovina without the knowledge of the Presidency of the Bosnia-Herzegovina. A delegation was set up, and it was composed of Biljana Plavsic, Ejub Ganic, and myself. And we did this in the space of two hours. We were quick to organise ourselves and to set up this delegation. We went to Belgrade straight away and we arrived at about 9.00 p.m. We took the plane, the presidency plane, to Belgrade and were there by 9.00 p.m. We went to the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, the building in Belgrade, but we were not received by the Federal Secretary himself, Mr. Kadijevic. We were received by his deputy, Admiral Brovet. And during the summer, the previous summer -- not the summer. During the flight in the plane, we had already decided to allow Biljana Plavsic to take the floor on our behalf and to talk to the person that we would be received by, that she would sort of represent us. This meeting was ten days before Vukovar was to fall, ten days before the fall of Vukovar into Serb hands. Vukovar fell on the 18th of November, 1991. So this might have been sometime around the 8th or 9th of the 11th, that is to say, our flight, our journey, the 8th, 9th of November, the 8th or 9th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, you were saying -- when you said "11th," "the 8th or 9th of the 11th," you were thinking about November, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: It was the 8th or 9th of November; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: May I ask you to give us the months and not the numbers of the months, because then the interpreters do not know whether you're referring to the 11th of a particular month or the 11th month of the year. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already said, we were received by Admiral Brovet. He gave us some coffee and we started our talks. Biljana Plavsic presented not the conclusion which we arrived in Belgrade with, but she put forward -- she started to actually praise the Yugoslav People's Army and not what we had agreed upon. She said that this was necessary and that the army is there to protect all the ethnic groups, all the nations, and she even went so far as almost to say that it should be decorated, they should be decorated and receive commendation for doing what they did. Now, after Biljana Plavsic had finished what she was saying, Ejub Ganic started to speak. He did so in slightly less emphatic terms, and he said, "Well, Admiral, what was done -- well, all right. Never mind," that sort of thing. "We in the presidency didn't know about it, but as it's fait accompli, what can we do? But in the future, we are the presidency. It would be a good idea if you would ask our opinion or inform us if you intend sending somebody, especially the army, to ask us what we think about it, to ask our permission, free passage through the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina." So he was very conciliatory, and he said, "Yes, Admiral, please refrain from doing what you did in the past." And then my turn came, and I presented the conclusions that we had reached previously in no uncertain terms. I was very decisive. I said, "Admiral, all the military units that you sent from Serbia and Montenegro to Bosnia-Herzegovina in part to stay in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the other portion going into Croatia, that's what you did. We demand that all those troops be returned along the same route. You should take the road back, the same road you took to come here, and that this should never happen again without consulting us." Of course, after that Admiral Brovet took the floor, and he held forth in a sort of monologue. He said that the Yugoslav People's Army was in Bosnia and Herzegovina to protect the population and all the nations and nationalities from -- in conflicts between themselves and amongst themselves. And they had distributed, of course, weapons to the Serb inhabitants and ensured the fact that the Serb side or 70 per cent of the -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina had been taken over through its SAO's, the SAO system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to that. But you just mentioned the SAO, SAO Krajina regions. Is that when these autonomous regions were formed? When were they actually formed, the SAO regions, the Serb autonomous regions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb autonomous regions began to be formed in the second half of 1991, and they were formed successively until the end of the year. All four Serb autonomous regions were formed during that period of time. There was the Nevesinje, the SAO Krajina, the Bijeljina area, the Romanija area, and the Banja Luka region, or whatever it was called, the Krajina there, the Bosanska Krajina. So there were the four Krajinas, SAO Krajinas, Serb autonomous regions Krajinas. And they covered about 80 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina territory. They already had their municipality authorities -- local authorities. And the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina and all the other laws and rules and regulations did not -- were not enforced in the territories of the Serb autonomous regions any more, and they were to become the Srpska Republika in January.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know when the community of Herceg-Bosna was formed, the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, and why was it formed, according to your knowledge? Could you tell us briefly something about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna was officially established on the 18th of November, 1991, which is to say precisely on the day that Vukovar fell. Now, why was it formed? Why was the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna formed in the first place? It was formed because of a notorious passivity on the part of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the main task of the presidency was to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the president's -- the presidency's foremost role. However, when, after having won the elections we became members of the presidency, the presidency had already lost all the basic premises for the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What do I mean when I say that? I mean that the JNA, knowing full well of these democratic changes that had taken place, especially the ones that took place in Slovenia first and then in Croatia, they knew that this was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well and that the League of Communists as a party would lose the elections. And knowing this, they disarmed the Territorial Defence, which was up until then under the command of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that the presidency faced with a situation of this kind had no military power, no military forces with which it would be able to set up any resistance to the Serb side, especially as it was such a well-armed and mighty side in the form of the Yugoslav People's Army. So that the Croatian people, as I said in view of the presidency's inability to act, its passive conduct, took it into their own hands to defend their municipalities, to defend their homes. And so it was in the municipalities that this resistance was first set up, not in a wholly organised manner. People procured weapons as they were able to, each person fending for themselves. Some of the Territorial Defence weapons had been hidden because the weapons belonging to the Territorial Defence were housed and stored in companies and in various places. So when the Yugoslav People's Army withdrew to -- withdrew, there were warehouses in Herzegovina, Central Bosnia, Northern Bosnia, Bosinska Posavina, and the people would seize these weapons and hide them because it was the people in the first place who paid for the purchase of those weapons. It was the citizens giving contributions via the local communities. So as this weaponry was built by portions of personal income set aside by the citizens themselves, they organised themselves in -- on the local community level, the municipality level, to seize these weapons and to hide them. And the need was found in free territory, on this 30 per cent of the territory that remained outside the control of the Serb side. People there, in that part of the territory, began to organise themselves. And we found that all this had to be coordinated, unified, that social life had to be organised as far as was possible, and that military resistance should be set up to the Serb side. The Serb side wasn't satisfied with holding 70 per cent of the territory. The Serb side, together with the JNA, wanted to move across Herzegovina, once again within the frameworks of this plan that was called RAM, R-A-M, to move across Herzegovina and Siroki Brijeg, Imotski, and to come to the rear of Split and Sibenik and Ploce, and to separate this southern portion of Croatia. And as I said, they'd already assumed control of Krajina up until Zadar. And had they succeeded in doing what they intended to do, there would no longer be any Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Bosnia-Herzegovina that we have today would no longer have existed. But it was thanks precisely to the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna that that 30 per cent of the territory was safeguarded and they were able to keep that part of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you take part in any of this? Did you hold an office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know what currency was used and what the relationship towards the other ethnic groups was between the HDSD and what the language was? And we'll come to the question of the Bosnian language a little bit later on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as money, currency, is concerned, there was several forms of legal tender, several currencies. Mostly it was the Deutschmark, the German mark, that prevailed in Bosnia, especially in Herzegovina during the times of Yugoslavia -- while it was still Yugoslavia and particularly during the war. But there were all sorts of currencies. There was the dinar, there was the kuna and others, but especially the convertible currencies. But as I say, the German mark was dominant and prevalent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you tell us what language was spoken and what the relationship was towards the other nationalities, the other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time it was the Croato-Serbian or Serbo-Croatian language that was used, and anybody in the area, whether he be a Croat, a Serb, a Muslim, it was all the same -- they were all the same. There was no difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Trial Chamber, please, whether the Bosnian language was in existence, did it exist. And if you could tell the Trial Chamber when the Muslim nation was created and when they were -- when they obtained their own -- got their own language.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, neither the Croats nor the Serbs nor the Bosniaks -- may I just explain something, with the Court's indulgence, at this point, please? May I explain something, Your Honours? Yes? May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I use the term "Muslim" or "the Muslim people," "the Muslim nation." I apologise to you, Your Honours, and to you gentlemen of the Defence and of the Prosecution because at that time, the time we are talking about, it was still referred to -- a Muslim was still referred to as being a Muslim of the Muslim nation, and a Bosniak or the Bosniak people or nation were introduced -- that term was introduced after the Washington Agreements, that is to say, the 18th of March, 1994; whereas the "Muslim nation," that term and concept was introduced pursuant to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina passed in 1974. The 1974 constitution provided for that category. Before that, the Muslim nation as such did not exist. What existed was the Muslims as believers, and they declared themselves either as Serbs or as Croats. But predominantly they would declare themselves as undetermined. And I thought it a good thing to -- for me to explain that to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What about the Bosnian language in that regard? Did it exist at all? Or when was it introduced? Could you tell us something about that. So I'm talking about the Bosniak language, not the Bosnian. The Bosniak language, when was that introduced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was introduced by the Washington Agreement on the 18th of March, as I said, 1994, when the Bosniak people as such were introduced. And analogously to that it was the Bosniak language for the Bosniak people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let me ask you, was it ever used or existed before 1992? Did the Bosnian language or the Bosniak language ever exist before that, between 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What was the school curriculum? What school programme and tuition programme did the children -- were the children taught?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends what they had found when they went to school. The textbooks were either in the Serbo-Croatian language or Croato-Serbian language, whatever version you like. And the children of all ethnic groups would receive tuition in the -- that language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you happen to know that there was -- whether there was any discrimination in the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna? Was anybody persecuted just for being a Muslim? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All I can say is that at that time, social life as we knew it had ceased because the -- with the advent of war. They were times of war. So the economy had stopped. And what economy there was, it was used for military purposes. Nobody worked; nobody went to work. The Serbs didn't work; the Croats didn't work; and the Muslims didn't go to work. So nobody could have any privileges. You couldn't have one side with privileges and not the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And now there were different talks and negotiations and proposals as to the internal system and set-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The war hadn't begun yet. There wasn't any fighting yet. So could you tell us of the influence that the International Community had at that time. What happened at that time in those days? Have you heard of the Badinter Commission, for example? Or what was the reaction of the International Community, generally speaking, to help you find a peaceful democratic solution to the problems at hand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the international community, at the proposal of the Badinter Commission, did amend and ascertained that the former republican boundaries or frontiers within the former Yugoslavia should become state borders, state boundaries and frontiers. That was the first thing. And the proposal to the Council of Europe made by the Badinter Commission was to recognise all the former republics, to recognise them in their former administrative borders, and to have them become independent states within those borders. But there was a three-month deferral period for Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro, Macedonia. As for Bosnia-Herzegovina, they said that Bosnia-Herzegovina must hold a referendum, and if the nations and nationalities or ethnic groups, through a referendum, opt for independence and sovereignty of their republic, then after that, after the referendum, the International Community would recognise their sovereignty, that is to say, the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And can you tell me whether this referendum was held and what was the result? Were only the external borders recognised in the referendum, and the political order within Bosnia and Herzegovina, was that something to be settled at a later date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, something strange happened. Only the Muslims and the Croats responded to the referendum. That was according to the census from 1991. According to that census, about 44 per cent were Muslims, 44 per cent of the population were Muslims, and the Croats accounted for 17 1/2 per cent. So that adds up to 61 per cent. Whereas the Serbian people didn't respond to the referendum. So those controlled by the Serbs, 70 per cent didn't go. All the Serbs in that part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was still not under their control, about 30 per cent, they didn't go to the referendum either. They didn't respond to the referendum. So the Croats and the Serbs -- the Croats and the Muslims went to the referendum - responded to the referendum. I apologise - and the vast majority, and especially the Croats, the vast majority of the Croats, went to the referendum. And there was a two-thirds majority. A two-thirds majority of the vote was obtained, and the conditions set by the International Community and the Council of Europe were met, the conditions for international recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but as a sort of external state, an external envelope, if I may put it this way. The recognition took place -- recognition was given on the 6th of April. The countries of the European community recognised the independence. This was in 1992. It all took place in that year. And in America, the USA, it was on the 7th that they recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina. But as soon as independence had been recognised and as soon as these conditions had been met with regard to the referendum, after that, the international community got involved immediately. They got involved in the internal order in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the internal system in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because the Serbian side had taken 70 per cent already, 30 per cent remained to the Croats and the Muslims, and the International Community took the position that: All right. So we have recognised the external borders, but the internal system, the internal order in Bosnia-Herzegovina, has to be settled. We have to find a solution to this. So first of all, the Security Council of the UN, in one of its resolutions, it made a response and it gave authority -- it extended authority to the Security Council of the United Nations. Their authority was extended from Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then there was Cutilhiero's plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I would like to take this in order, Witness. Sorry for interrupting you. I would like to ask you: Could you tell this Trial Chamber, do you know whether the Croats -- if the Croats had not responded to the referendum, would Bosnia-Herzegovina have been recognised as an independent state, as it is today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In such a case, what would have happened to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know, but it would have remained -- in my personal opinion, it would have remained within -- as part of Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now that the talks started about the future political order, were you personally, the things that you personally participated in, did you go to talk to other presidents perhaps, Milosevic or Tudjman, under the auspices of the international community, or in Geneva? And what were the proposals, and were the proposals allowed in the sense of democratically settling the future political order? So this is just before Badinter, before the recognition of independence, because after that we know that war broke out and we know what happened subsequently. So if you could provide us with some personal information about all of this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In an attempt to avoid a large-scale war -- and by that time there were individual, local wars, especially between the Croatian population and the JNA. We mentioned Ravno and Kupres and the area around Bosanski Brod, and also in Central Bosnia, around Busovaca. There were local incidents that had started breaking out. We can consider those to be incidents. Let's call them in this manner. What I wanted to do, and certain others too, was in order to avoid a large-scale war, we wanted to try and find a solution. In an attempt to do this, I remember very well on the 8th of January, 1992, Mr. Koljevic phoned me from Belgrade, sometime about 12.00. So this was at midday. He asked me whether I could organise a meeting for him with Mr. Tudjman and his associates. I wasn't able to answer him immediately. He gave me about half an hour so that I could phone Tudjman and the others, and I really did phone President Tudjman. And his reply was, "You can come immediately. I would be glad if Mr. Boras could tell me what it has to do with." I said, "I don't know either. Koljevic didn't tell me why he was asking for a meeting." But he said, "Come." So I told Koljevic about this, or rather, he phoned me again. I told him that President Tudjman wanted us to come. And in the meantime, while he was coming, while he was travelling from Belgrade, while he was flying to Sarajevo, I went to the -- I was with the general secretary, Mile Akmadzic, and he was the only one who had the right to issue an order to pilots and to those involved in flights and to the members of the presidency. He could give us travel authorisation. I dealt with all of this in the meantime. We left about half past 4.00. The presidency and the administration was not working at that time. Working hours were up until 3.00, so that we and the crew, the flight crew, we left about half past 4.00. We took off about half past 4.00. We arrived there about half past 5.00, as far as I can remember. We arrived in the president's building at about 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Zagreb. President Tudjman did not meet us there. We weren't received by President Tudjman, but it was the Prime Minister, Mr. Manolic, with, as far as I can remember, his associates, Mr. Susak, Nerotic Ramljak, and I don't know whether anyone else was there. In the course of the flight, I asked Mr. Koljevic why he wanted this meeting. I asked him whether he had some sort of document, a proposal. He said, "I don't have a proposal of any kind. I have nothing on paper, but I have something in my head." I asked him again, "Does Mr. Milosevic know anything about what you have in your head?" I told him a few things and he didn't agree with that. But I told him, "In spite of that, I want to talk to President Tudjman to see what his opinion is, to see whether there was any point in talking about this, discussing this further." I knew that Mr. Koljevic, throughout the year 1991, he was working to implement a sort of Swiss model in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the other members of the presidency were inundated with such material which had this as its goal. He had been studying the state system in Switzerland, the way it was ordered, and he liked this, and he thought that perhaps something could be done in that sense in Bosnia and Herzegovina too, but in a democratic way, and the reason for this was to avoid war with the Muslims. He knew that I supported this and I liked this solution too, given that there were three peoples there, and we spoke in a pure language, so to speak, and dammit, that would be the best, to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina into cantons. And in some cantons, the Serbs would be in the majority; in other cantons, Muslims would be in the majority, and so on. And we would have a sort of central authority, a central government which would be organised in a rational way. "Well, look, Nikola," I said, "that's a great idea." But then he told me, "Mr. Boras, I'm not a lawyer. I'm a literary man. Could you help me a bit when we arrive at the talks with Tudjman? Could you help me with this a bit, help me to present this, to say what this should look like?" And I said, "Gladly, Mr. Koljevic."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see that it is 10.15, and we will be moving to the subject of these transcripts now, so perhaps it would be good to have a pause, a break now, because I have finished with one part. With your permission, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes. This is the right time. We'll resume at a quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Bring in the witness, please. Yes, Mr. Krsnik. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, the last thing we were talking about was the meeting in Zagreb. The last thing you said was that you went to see Mr. Tudjman; you were received by Mr. Manolic. And perhaps you could briefly say what the dialogue was about, what you talked about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Koljevic -- well, what he had in his head, he tried to convey this to the hosts. And as far as I can remember -- but we must bear in mind the fact that the Serbian side had already taken -- had already occupied over 70 per cent of the territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He suggested to the Croatian side in Zagreb that within the framework of Bosnia and Herzegovina, one should establish three states and that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be a federal state. I said he was a literary man. He wasn't a lawyer. But when he made this proposal, when he proposed this solution, he would sometimes mention the Swiss model for internal, political, and state organisation. He would mention this model for Bosnia and Herzegovina. But very often he would get confused. He would -- there would be some confusion as to whether it would be three states with three peoples, and that each of those states or statelets, so Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Croatian state, the Muslim State of Bosnia and Herzegovina, each one would have fairly strong ties: The Croatian state in BH with the Croatian republic; the Serbian state would have close ties with Yugoslavia, that is to say with Serbia and Montenegro; and the Muslim state in Bosnia and Herzegovina would be as it wanted to be. It would be up to the -- the Muslim state whether it would have closer ties with Croatia, with Serbia and Montenegro, and even it would be up to them to decide whether they should have closer ties with a state beyond the borders of the former Yugoslavia. So it's necessary to understand that these talks -- these were talks. They weren't negotiations. It wasn't a matter of trying to reach an agreement. They were talks, the purpose of which was to clarify a certain conception which Koljevic presented in a fairly confused manner at that meeting. What then followed from the hosts, the Croatian representatives, were various questions. They put various questions as to whether he had this idea developed somewhere, questions relating to how he would implement this, how this would be implemented. And he then said that this idea, if it were to come to life, if it were to function, it would be necessary to first reconstruct the municipalities, carry out a reconstruction of the municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the system of the municipalities there at the time of when the communists were in power, it was badly organised and -- to the detriment to the Croats and of the Serbs. So that -- we're talking about this conception, this idea of his with which he came to Zagreb. In order to talk about it, in order to discuss this idea, it would be necessary to reconstruct the municipal system, and this should be in the favour of Croats and the Serbs, because the municipal organisation at the time favoured the Muslim people. So as far as I can remember, they mentioned -- as far as I can remember, I mentioned two municipalities in particular which as they were at the time did not favour the Croats. They were established at that time, and they did not favour the Croats. And Koljevic also mentioned Banja Luka, and I mentioned Dobratici. That's an area. It has perhaps between four and five thousand inhabitants. And before the municipal organisation carried out by the communists, by the communist authorities, Dobratici was part of the area of Travnik, of old Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, I do apologise for interrupting you, and I do respect your age, but I would like to ask you if you could be a little more concise. Could we just focus on that dialogue that took place there. Could you tell the Trial Chamber about what happened there, in a few sentences.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that this reorganisation of the municipalities should have been the grounds on which this could be sort of reconstructed, the grounds on which one could develop the option that Mr. Koljevic had presented and talked about. So the two municipalities that I have mentioned -- Dobratici was taken away from the municipality of Travnik and it became part of the municipality of Kulen Vakuf, and in that way the municipality of Travnik had the Muslim people in a majority. And in Kulen Vakuf -- and in Dobratici and Kulen Vakuf, the Croats were in the minority there. Or let's say Mostar. In Mostar, a village with three or four thousand Croatian inhabitants, was -- it's called Luti Dolac [phoen]. It was taken away from Mostar, the municipality of Mostar, and it became part of Siroki Brijeg, where the Croatian population was in the majority, even without Luti Dolac. And from Jablanica -- a village somewhere up there was taken away from Jablanica. It was taken away from Jablanica and joined Mostar, and that's how Mostar -- Mostar had the Muslim population in the majority as far as these villages surrounding the town are concerned, and so on. So I want to say that the Communist system attempted to make as many urban areas as possible. They attempted to ensure that the Muslim people were in the majority in those areas, and the Serbs and the Muslims in those urban areas were to be in minority [as interpreted]. So after these discussions, as far as I can remember, the question was how this option that Koljevic had suggested, how this option would be established, how it would be given life, what its raison d'etre would be. And we saw that no preparations had been done for that and that we could only talk about this option. And then the conclusion was drawn that when we returned to Sarajevo, professional teams should be formed in order to attempt to put this all down on paper, to study this option, and having studied this, to see whether it would at all be possible, given the conditions at the time, whether it would be possible to implement such an option.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, how did this idea of federalisation go down, the one that Mr. Koljevic suggested and the one that he presented in Zagreb? How did the Serbian side react? How did Milosevic react?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This idea cropped up and it disappeared in a similar manner. When we returned to Sarajevo, Koljevic informed Karadzic. He also said in Zagreb that his people - and that meant Milosevic, Karadzic, et cetera - he said that they didn't know about this idea of his. And he told Karadzic what he had spoken about, what he had discussed. He told him this in my presence. And at that point Karadzic said that he had to inform Milosevic of this, he had to tell Milosevic about this idea, and when he returned, that he would inform us about this. The following day, I informed Mr. Kljuic, the president - he was still the president of the Croatian Democratic Union at that time and a member of the presidency - I informed him of the subject of our conversations, and in the afternoon I informed the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, of this. I provided him with all the details that had been discussed. And Kljuic, in particular, asked me, "Well, why did you go there? Why did you go to Zagreb without my being aware of this?" And first of all, we left at about half past 4.00. There was no one in the presidency at that time. Kljuic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sorry. Did you have to inform him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have to inform him, because we were equal. The president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic too, he is the first among equals. So each member of the presidency can act independently, but it is necessary to subsequently inform the presidency what was discussed. And I even asked President Izetbegovic to put this on the agenda, to put such an option on the agenda, which at that time -- this option at that time, it would have been great if it had come to life, if it had functioned. There wouldn't have been a war if it had been implemented. But I must say one other thing: Having returned from Belgrade, Karadzic told Mr. Koljevic that this option would come to nothing, that Milosevic hadn't accepted that plan, that option, and that we wouldn't be undertaking anything to this effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Do you know whether there were any minutes from that meeting in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that it was being taped, but I never received a transcript of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm going to show you the transcript that we received from the Prosecution, and the number is ASPT/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher's assistance, please, to hand round copies. [In English] It's formerly admitted PT/3, presidential transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we cannot find it. Before your trial we were furnished with a list, but on that list we did not find that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Your Honour. My colleague has just told me that there has been an error. Of course, this is an important document, and I can see that it's not on the list myself. Well, if that makes it impossible to follow now, perhaps I'll come back to it at a later stage in due course during a break, if I may be allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Boras, while we're looking for the document for the Trial Chamber, the transcript, we'll go on to something else and we'll come back to that. You'll be able to have a look at it later on and tell us whether that is indeed the transcript of the conversation you had. To move on: Tell me now, please, if you know, whether there were any other initiatives. Did you talk to other party presidents or members of political parties? Did you have any meetings with SDA leaders? Did you talk to Alija, Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Cehajic? Before Bosnia was recognised, what proposals were put on the table?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was something similar to the proposal put forward by Mr. Koljevic that he offered to the Croatian side. We and the Croatian side, Mr. Milenko Brkic, who was the charge d'affaires of the Croatian Democratic Community Union, we offered a similar proposal and put it before the Muslim side. And if I may say so, we had a better-prepared proposal for the Muslim side than Koljevic had to present to the Croatian side. We'd worked it out better. And there was a meeting in the cabinet of the president, of the presiding individual, which was -- who was Alija Izetbegovic. We met with Mahmut Cehajic -- Rusmir Mahmut Cehajic. At that time he was an ideologist of the Muslims and was also a minister. He was Minister of Energy, I think, in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And this conception of ours was in broad terms, broadly speaking, the following: That the Muslim and Croatian side should offer the Serb side, the Serbs -- and I'm talking about territorial separation -- that the Serbs should be given all the municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina where there was a majority Serb population, an absolute Serb majority, and that the Muslim and Croatian side should be given the rest of the municipalities, that is to say, where the Muslims and Croats in turn formed the absolute majority population compared to the Serbs. This proposal would be presented -- and as far as territorial division is concerned -- and that was the main problem always among these three nationalities or ethnic groups. It was always to do with the territorial problem. That was always the key. According to our -- that concept, the Serb side would have been given about 32 per cent of the territory, roughly speaking, which according to the last population census was how many Serbs inhabited Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I'm referring to the 1991 population census. The Muslim and Croat side should have got about 68 per cent of the territory, thereabouts. Now, this 68 per cent, we would have to decide amongst ourselves, that is to say, amongst the Muslims and Croats, as to how this should be divided, because the two of us, the Croats and Muslims, were still on one side against the Serb side because the Serbs with the JNA had occupied about 70 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So the Muslim and Croat side, according to that proposal of ours, would have received about 68 per cent. Now, of that 68 per cent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I'm going to ask for a bit more information, please. There's a lot of things being discussed. There's no parameters as to date, time, or place, or exactly who is participating in these discussions, when. I invite the Chamber to look at the screen over the last some lines of answers. There's a lot being put on the table, so to speak. I don't know if we're now talking in broad sweeps of things that happened somewhere over a three-year period, we're talking about a series -- a composite of -- a series of meetings. I think we're going to have to take this in a little bit more specific order of what conversation, with who, of what dates, and where, what -- move on to the next meeting and have a little more specifics as to what we're talking about. That's our request, anyway, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And also who was involved in the meeting. I didn't want to interrupt because I thought the witness would come round to it, but it's very important to know who was negotiating at the meeting. I'm sure it wasn't Mr. Boras on his own for the Croat community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think you should put all those in your questions. You could ask some questions specifically concerning with the time, the place, and the person involved in all those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honours. I -- my sequence was logical. The first meeting was in Zagreb. This second meeting -- and I am doing my best to follow the transcript. At that second meeting, there was a representative of the SDA. And his name was Rusmir Mahmut Cehajic. I don't know whether that was entered into the transcript. And on -- and then there -- on the other side was the charge d'affaires of the president, Mr. Brkic, and Mr. Boras on the HDZ side, and Alija Izetbegovic represented the Muslims. I'm trying to follow the transcript. As to the date, Mr. Boras is speaking rather slowly. And I don't like to interrupt him, respecting the fact that Mr. Boras is my senior. I think he might lose the thread of what he's saying. But I have tried to ask him to focus on the question and to be briefer. But may I ask the Court's indulgence for the way in which the witness is answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, you have heard the guidelines given by the Trial Chamber. Could you give us some dates, please, tell us the date and where it took place. I'm sure you intended to say that. But before we begin, can you tell us the date and place of the meeting and then what was discussed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first meeting with Mr. Rusmir Mahmut Cehajic was in the cabinet, took place in the president -- in the presidency's office, Alija Izetbegovic. And it took place --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Just a moment, Witness. Could you kindly spell the name, because it is difficult for our interpreters and the transcript. Could you spell the name, first and last name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rusmir Mahmut Cehajic is the name. And the meeting took place in the cabinet of the president of the presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. The meeting was held at the end of March 1992. And on our side, the participants were the deputy president of the Croatian Democratic Union, Milenko Brkic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No. I apologise. It said "deputy president" in the transcript, but DB is the charge d'affaires, the charge d'affaires of the Croatian Democratic Union. And I will spell the surname. M-a -- no, the first name. The charge d'affaires was Mr. Milenko. The acting president, actually, the acting president was Mr. Milenko, M-i-l-e-n-k-o, Brkic, B-r-k-i-c. Brkic is the surname: B-r-k-i-c. And on the opposite side, the negotiator was Mr. R-u-s-m-i-r, Rusmir; and the next name is M-a-h-m-u-t; and the next name is C-u-h -- C-e-h -- C-e-h- -- Cehajic, C-e-h-a-j-i-c diacritic. That's it for purposes of the transcript and record. I apologise for interrupting you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I think you should give some guidance to this witness. You know, the witness is not that experienced as you. He did not know how this trial is functioning, especially from the different legal systems. So you could give some more guidance to your witness through your question. And as we understand, that this witness now is mainly testified on the background issues in which you're allowed to ask some leading questions. You may proceed, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, could you briefly explain to us the platform represented by Mr. Mahmut Cehajic and which was your platform.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that on the Croatian side, we presented that the -- we said that the Muslim and Croatian side should make a joint presence vis-a-vis the Serb side, in the sense of offering the Serb side jointly, for our part, 32 per cent of the territory. And it was the territory with Serb majority municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And could you tell us the political platform that Mr. Mahmut Cehajic advocated.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mahmut Cehajic, in the presence of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, did not want to accept this concept because he, as he had been earlier on, remained on his previous political platform and position. In practice, that is to say, from the elections right up to that time, he advocated the fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina must be united, unitarian, without any constituent units, especially not federal ones. Something along the lines of being a bourgeois republic, following along the lines of what Milosevic had asked for. Milosevic wanted this to be Yugoslavia based on the principles of one citizen, one vote. And he wanted this to hold true for Bosnia-Herzegovina as well. However, a concept of this kind would have been all right for the type of Bosnia-Herzegovina in which one nation were -- had at least a two-thirds majority, compared to the other ethnic groups who lived and inhabited that kind of republic. We had a second meeting a little later. The war had already begun, so it might have been sometime between the 15th -- or rather, the 10th and the 15th of April, 1992. And we met in my cabinet, in my office. And representing our side, along with me, was once again the acting president of the Croatian Democratic Union. His name was Milenko Brkic. And Mahmut -- Rusmir Mahmut Cehajic came to the meeting. It was our intention to discuss the concept once again, and all this in the aim of avoiding the war which had actually already begun throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. But nonetheless, we decided to make one more effort for our part to do our utmost to prevent it from flaring up and to be able to do the right thing as regards history, and to offer solutions which we thought we would be able to present to the Serbian side and have them prevail. Unfortunately, and to the detriment of all three ethnic groups, especially the Croat nationality, this concept was not found acceptable by the Muslim side. Rusmir Mahmut Cehajic once again refused to accept this kind of decentralised concept for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he once again insisted that Bosnia-Herzegovina could not be divided. He kept referring to the leopard skin and spotty type of territory, that it had to have a constitutional order in which the one-citizen, one-vote principle would prevail. And on that basis, the national question would have completely been forgotten and left to one side. And as the Croatian people were in the minority in Bosnia-Herzegovina but they were constituent and equal with the other two nations, we thought that it was important for Bosnia and Herzegovina to be organised and established in such a way as would make all three ethnic groups equal, that they would all be on a footing of equality. And that is why we were open to all solutions which would arrive at that goal. And later on, the international community put forward different plans and programmes, and they were all along those lines. They all said that Bosnia-Herzegovina could not be established on a unitary basis but that it had to recognise the rights of all three nations or ethnic groups and have a social and political legal order in which all three nationalities or ethnic groups would feel at home and equal with all the other -- with the other two ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: This brings us to the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina's external borders. Now, what happened next? What decisions were made? Could you tell us a bit about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the referendum, Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised, which gave rise to the Serb side to leave the position of authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They left the presidency, they left the Assembly, they stepped down from the government, they stepped down from the Constitutional Court, from the Supreme Court, in a word, all the organs of power and authority in which they had participated thus far. What we saw now was a very strange situation, a strange state of affairs. We were elected. We assumed power, according to the constitution, according to a constitution which the former system, the Communist system, had adopted in 1974, with 79 amendments to it, up until 1990. The presidency, when the two members had left - that is to say, Mrs. Biljana Plavsic and Mr. Nikola Koljevic - was left with just five members: three Muslims, two Croats, and that was it. There was myself, there was Mr. Kljuic, and the three Muslims: Alija Izetbegovic, Ejub Ganic, and Abdic. Faced with a situation of this kind, once again, pursuant to the 1974 constitution which was enacted by the Communist authorities in their day -- and we were a democratic power. The democratic power wanted to overthrow this whole system, Communist system, and order. However, in 1991, we were not able to do so. We did not succeed in that. We did not change a single institution. And in our presidency, we were not even able to let go one of the clerks at the reception desk, let alone anybody else. We found 16 advisors, counsellors, there that had been nominated and appointed by the former Communist authorities, and they were our advisors throughout that time. So they were former Communists now acting as advisors to a democratically elected government. The 1974 constitution, along with its amendments, provided for the fact that in a situation where the Assembly is no longer able to function -- because it was wartime, the assembly was unable to meet, to convene. According to the constitution and rules and regulations governing the work of the Presidency, they provided for the establishment of a War Presidency, and a War Presidency would include the regular members of the presidency - that is to say, the five of us who remained within the presidency - plus the President of the Assembly, who was in power - the Prime Minister, the head of government, in other words - and the commander of the Territorial Defence. That's what the law provided. Now, what was the situation at that particular point in time? At that point in time, the President of the Assembly, as you saw on the photograph earlier on, we were taking the oath of office, but it was Momcilo Krajisnik who also left the Assembly, who stepped down from the Assembly to go to the Republic of Serbia and be President of the Assembly of Serbia. So he stepped down. Then you saw the Prime Minister, who was a Croat, and according to the constitutional provisions, he could become member of the War Presidency. But the constitution and rules of procedure also provided for the fact that the commander of the Territorial Defence become a member of the War Presidency. But what happened there? Let's take a look at that office. The commander of the Territorial Defence was Dragan Vukosavljevic. He was a Serb. So he left in March 1992, his post and office. He retired. He stepped down from active service, retired, and went to Belgrade. And Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there was no Territorial Defence either. That was abolished. I think I said earlier on that the Territorial Defence was disbanded, dismantled, and that the weapons were seized by the Yugoslav People's Army that had belonged to the TO and had been stored in their warehouses and was later on distributed to the Serb population. We learnt that later on, the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that we now have -- we were now faced with this kind of situation, and the external explanation and interpretation of this newly arisen sort of constitutional or unconstitutional state of affairs - whatever you like to call it - what happened was that in the Presidency, there were three members, three Croats, us three Croats, plus Jure Pelivan, the Prime Minister at the time, and three Muslim members: Alija Izetbegovic, Abdic, and Ejub Ganic. So that -- now, as the Croats and Muslims had gone to the referendum and received Bosnia-Herzegovina's recognition, that could have remained as it was. However, in view of the fact that the President of the Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik, had left and gone to the Republic of Serbia, the presidency decided, as the Assembly was unable to meet, therefore, according to the constitution, the War Presidency could enact laws or bills, draft laws or bills having the force of law. And this is what we did. As the President of the Assembly, a Serb, had left, and his replacement was Mariofil Ljubic. He was a Croat. So he joined -- he could -- he was eligible to become a member of the War Presidency. As far as the TO commander was concerned, this was a question and issue to be decided on by the HDZ, Croatian Democratic Union, and the SDA, the Party of Democratic Action, amongst themselves. They were to decide how the question of defence, the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, with the War Presidency at its head, should be conducted. So what happened next? With Mariofil Ljubic as the vice-president of the Assembly to Momcilo Krajisnik in the War Presidency, there were now four Croats and three Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Boras. I will guide you a little further. Could you please tell us what happened in the end to this TO commander, Territorial Defence commander. Did he come? Who elected him? According to the presidency, was this constitutional? And later on, how did Mr. Kecmanovic come to the presidency? What happened with that presidency? You mentioned the establishment of a War Presidency. What was the situation in Sarajevo and in the BH? When was the War Presidency established? Could you be brief, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the War Presidency was established -- I think that was on the 6th of April, 1992. And the declaration of a state of war was on the 4th of April, 1992, although in other areas outside of Sarajevo, the war had been going on, well, according to me, from the 6th of May, 1991, from Graz and further on. But the official declaration of war was on the 6th of April, 1992. On the 6th of April -- in April of that year, the regular presidency met, first of all, and then, on the basis of constitutional authority, a War Presidency was formed such as I have described it. We then issued a second decree law in which we said that instead of the members leaving in any way, members of the regular War Presidency leaving in any way, we said that they could -- that the following members or candidates could enter the War Presidency, those who were candidates in elections on the 18th of November, 1990, in accordance with the following results in the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Who then entered the presidency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in accordance with this decree law, instead of the members of the Serbian people who had left - Nikola Koljevic, Biljana Plavsic - instead of them, the following entered the War Presidency: Nenad Kecmanovic and Pejanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you tell me whether they remained in the presidency for the entire period, all the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pejanovic remained there all the time, and Nenad Kecmanovic, he was there for very brief period of time. I think that in July 1992 he left and went to Belgrade. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was he replaced by someone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was replaced by Tatjana Ljujic-Mijatovic, who was not a candidate for the Presidency. She wasn't the candidate of any party in 1990. So on the 18th of November, 1991, she wasn't a candidate for the presidency, and therefore, according to this decree law which we issued, which the War Presidency issued, according to this decree law, she should not have been in a position to replace Nenad Kecmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you please tell us why the Constitutional Court did not cancel this appointment? And who appointed her, in any case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, she was appointed by Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: On the basis of what provision? On the basis of what law?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no provisions for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did the Constitutional Court react?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could it have reacted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you tell me what happened - and very briefly, to deal with this issue of the presidency - what happened to the Croatian members of the presidency?
