utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a little later, on the 8th -- in August or September - I don't know exactly - Stjepan Kljuic, who was elected to represent the Croatian people - he was a candidate of the HDZ - he resigned. He was replaced by the Croat Miro Lasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did he come on the basis of some rules or provisions? Could he have been a member?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with Mr. Kljuic in some of his statements that he made. He said that Miro Lasic was picked up in the street, because he wasn't a candidate for the presidency and he wasn't even a member in the parliament. But he was in the government on some political basis because this was suitable. How he got there, how he became a member of the War Presidency, there was some sort of secret agreements between Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban. I'm not familiar with them. But in any event, they are suspicious.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly request that counsel make pauses between question and answer, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The War Presidency kept to Sarajevo. They followed the reasoning of Alija Izetbegovic, which was that he would defend Sarajevo, even if this was at the cost of 300.000 casualties. And if he managed to defend Sarajevo, that in such a case, he would manage to defend Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, just before the 1st of May, 1992, I received a call from Mostar, from the headquarters for the defence of Mostar, the defence of Mostar against the JNA and the Serbian and Montenegrin reservists. I was called to come to a meeting because they had arranged for a meeting with -- that headquarters had arranged for a meeting with General Perisic, a general in the JNA, which had surrounded and which was shelling Mostar. I received that message quite late on in the evening, and I informed Milenko Brkic of this and asked him if he could -- at the time he was still the president of the HDZ - I asked him if he could organise this trip, because Sarajevo had been blocked by the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very briefly, could you tell us whether there was electricity, whether telephones were functioning? What was the situation in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll just finish this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could we just be a bit more rapid, because time is precious.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to Mostar on the 1st of May at 7.00. We were escorted -- we were with the chiefs of the European Mission, Santos, and a colonel in the JNA who had relations with -- who maintained relations between the European observers, the European monitors, and the JNA. As we were with them, we were able to get through the JNA positions in Sarajevo, and we entered the eastern part of Mostar also through the JNA and Serbian positions. We got to that meeting and we waited for the general. We waited for General Perisic for five hours. We called him on the phone. We asked him to come to the meeting. He didn't come, and so that meeting was not successful. I was not able to return to Sarajevo because this colonel -- this general went to Belgrade via Nevesinje, and Santos, the chief of the monitors, also went to Nevesinje, and they would take some other route. So I had to stay in Mostar. At that time, there was chaos in Sarajevo. Sarajevo had been surrounded on all sides. It was being shelled. All the areas were being shelled, so that we barely managed to get out alive, to get out from Sarajevo alive. And this was again thanks to those checkpoints manned by the Serbs and the JNA. Near Kiseljak -- the last checkpoint was near Kiseljak. At that checkpoint they wanted to confiscate my car and detain my driver, but the colonel of the JNA intervened, and after his intervention they let me through to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was the HVO formed at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Even before I had gone to Mostar on the 8th of April, 1992, the HVO was formed. And three or four days later, a fax arrived, as far as I know, containing a proposal from the HVO, and it was a proposal sent to the presidency, a proposal to form joint quarters for the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- joint staff for the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And this would be between the military forces of the HVO and the Territorial Defence, which at the presidency -- which we had founded at the presidency, too. And this Territorial Defence would very soon be turned into the army of BH. This proposal was given to us by the presiding individual, Alija Izetbegovic. It was shown to us by him. He showed it to us, told us that it had arrived from the HVO. But he said that we couldn't discuss the proposal because he wasn't ready, but that when he was ready, he said that we would discuss it. That might have been on the 10th or the 11th of April. And every day we -- there were sessions of the War Presidency, both in the morning and the afternoon, right up until I left on the 1st of May, 1992. And on several occasions, I insisted that we should discuss this proposal that had been sent by the HVO. However, Alija Izetbegovic always avoided this. He would always say that it hadn't been prepared, that there was time for that, et cetera. But in addition to the War Presidency, Hasan Efendic was always present. He was the commander of the Territorial Defence. And he gave us -- he provided us with some information about Sarajevo, about what was happening in Sarajevo, and about those Serbian forces there. But it only had to do with Sarajevo and what was happening in Sarajevo. He was not in a position to provide us with information on what was happening outside the confines of Sarajevo and in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that that proposal that came from the HVO was never officially discussed at the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So after the War Presidency had been established and everything that had happened, did you meet and did you personally talk to Alija Izetbegovic about the political reality and about what it was necessary to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during those everyday meetings which took place in the morning and in the afternoon and late at night -- at the time there was a lot of shooting around Sarajevo and in Sarajevo. Quite a few of those sessions were held in the cell of the presidency building because we were always expecting to be shelled from the surrounding hills. And Alija and I -- well, we were raised in a religious way. And so on that basis, we -- we would be glad to speak to each other because of that while we were waiting for official sessions. And on one or two occasions, he told me, "Listen, Franjo, we'll defend Sarajevo. And if we defend Sarajevo, then the entire -- the entire -- all of Bosnia and Herzegovina could fall into enemy hands. But if we defend Sarajevo, we will have defended Bosnia and Herzegovina too. And I'm ready to accept 300.000 victims and to accept a million people who might be expelled. But if we do -- if we act in this way that I'm thinking of, we will remain in the majority, in comparison to the Croatian and Serbian people, so that in spite of everything, we will be the main force in Bosnia and Herzegovina; we will have the majority in Bosnia and Herzegovina." And on the other said, he would say, "Look, Franjo, the -- we're barely 1.700.000." But as far as the Efendi said -- and "Efendi" in Turkish means gentleman -- I said, "Efendi Alija, how many Muslims are there? Over 1.700.000?" Well, he said, "Franjo, over a billion." "What do you mean a billion," I said, "Alija, my friend?" "Well," he said, "there aren't blood ties between us Muslims. It's not blood that connects us. It is religion that connects us. The way I think in Sarajevo is the way that people in Saudi Arabia, Indonesia, and in Algeria think." I said, "Well, Alija, what does this mean? This does not bode well because you are -- you are the people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's not just religion that connects you. What should connect you -- there should be more connecting you to us Croats and to the Serbs than to those people in Indonesia and Pakistan and to the way in which they think in those eastern countries." Well, he said, "Listen, Franjo, that's the way we think about this matter. And if it is necessary, there will be fighters, soldiers from those -- soldiers, and as many as necessary."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did Alija -- had Alija previously expressed such ideas before 1990, and did he go to prison because of those ideas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't read that Islamic declaration of his. But I know that because of that Islamic declaration, he had been brought to trial and that that Islamic declaration had been incorporated into the political programme of the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell me whether you went to any other meetings -- and the war had broken out, the international community was also getting involved. Did you go to any other meetings -- and I will be specific, if the Trial Chamber allows me to be so. Did you go to a meeting in Graz where the Serbian delegation was being led by Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When I said "Graz," I am thinking of Austria. And could you please mention the date the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was -- when I was unable to return on the 1st of May, 1992, to return from Mostar where I had gone because of the meeting that I spoke about earlier on, on the 2nd I reported -- on the 2nd of May of that same year, I reported to Mate Boban in Gruda. I told him that I had arrived in Mostar and that I could not return to Sarajevo but that I remained -- that I was still a member of the presidency and that at that time I could still contact with him before establishing contact with Sarajevo. And on that occasion, he told me, "Well, that's fine. That's fine. We'll -- on the 6th of May, we will -- on the 6th of May, 1992, we will be going to Graz to a meeting with the Serbian representatives, Mr. Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, and the regional SDS member, Branko -- Branko Simic." But before this meeting, there is another meeting in Sarajevo that I should mention, because this was the continuation of a discussion about Cutilheiro's plan. And on the 22nd of April, 1992, I headed the Croatian delegation, and I took them to the talks at the Butmir airport. These talks were with the international delegation headed by the Ambassador Pinjarino [phoen], and Cutilheiro and Lord Carrington were there. These discussions also had to do with Cutilheiro's plan. In particular, Alija Izetbegovic headed the Muslim delegation with his associates. And the Serbian delegation was headed by Karadzic. I headed the Croatian delegation because Boban was not able to come, as Sarajevo had been blockaded. Milenko Brkic was also supposed to head the delegation. I was supposed to be a member of the delegation. But he was afraid because there was shooting everywhere and it was necessary to get to Butmir from the centre of Sarajevo and to pass all those checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Butmir is the airport?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Butmir airport in Sarajevo. And in the building at the airport in Butmir, that's where the talks were held. And at those meetings -- at that meeting, that was the last meeting in the presence of the international community. And I'm talking about Cutilheiro's plan. We were then told that the international community, in further talks about Cutilheiro's plan -- the international community would not be present. We were told that we should try to find a solution on our own and between ourselves, a solution with regard to the territorial division of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because this territorial division had only remained a matter of contention. Everything else, what concerns the social and legal order of Bosnia and Herzegovina in accordance with Cutilheiro -- Cutilheiro's plans, this had been agreed on. It was supposed to be a cantonal system, and there were supposed to be three constituent entities. Everything had to be agreed on to the government and to other areas. But what was contentious was territory. They told us, "Please carry on the talks about the territory. And if you come to an agreement, that's fine." Then at the end, Mr. Carrington said, "Mr. Boras, if you don't reach an agreement, we will let you kill each other. We will let you destroy whatever remains to be destroyed. And then we will impose a solution." I raised my hands, and I said -- I told Lord Carrington, "Well, Lord Carrington, how can we reach an agreement? Look, we are surrounded in Sarajevo. We're talking to the Serbian side that has 70 per cent -- that controls 70 per cent of the territory. It has vast quantities of weapons. It has the Yugoslav People's Army," which at the time was, in terms of military power, the fourth -- the fourth force in Europe. "How can we reach an agreement? I don't know," I said. "I told you. Make an effort. If you don't reach an agreement, then it bodes ill for you." And these talks in Graz were the continuation of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Before Graz, was Cutilheiro's plan signed? Was it signed before Graz or after Graz?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was signed as far as the social and legal order is concerned. But as far as the territorial division is concerned, that remained a contentious issue and it wasn't signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And then you went to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We went to negotiate without the presence of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you went to a meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to a meeting in Graz. And on that morning, we left for Zagreb quite early. We got there in my -- we went there in my official car. It was a Golf with a Sarajevo -- with Sarajevo number plates. In Zagreb, we had to change cars because we couldn't carry on -- we couldn't get through the Slovenian border with a Sarajevo number plate. The Ministry of Defence of Croatia gave us a Croatian car, and we were able to get to the airport with this car -- in this car. We were able to get to the building of the Graz airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Graz is in which country?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Austria. The date was the 6th of May, 1992. In the Croatian delegation -- the former president in the Croatian delegation, Mate Boban, Vlado Santic, and myself, we waited for the Serbian delegation. They arrived -- we got there about 10.00, maybe 11.00. And they were about one hour late.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When you say "they," you mean who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian side: Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, and Branko Simic. They got there by plane.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you please stop because it's time for a pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that 75 minutes have gone by. If the Trial Chamber would allow us to do so, we might take a break now and then continue. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Have you had a rest, Witness? I hope so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Because of our time constraints, may I ask you once again to try and concentrate on the main issues and events that I am asking about. If you could do your best to focus on them. Thank you for your understanding. We left off with Graz, and you were saying that the Serb delegation led by Karadzic had arrived at Graz airport. Now, my question would be - and you can tell us what you talked about - namely, we have heard in this courtroom that you were discussing the question, that is to say, the Serbs and Croats to divide up Bosnia and that the Bosnians should wind up in the Neretva River, if I can put it that way. So was anything signed? Was any agreement put down on paper? And could you say a few words about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we discussed the territorial division of the country in conformity with Cutilheiro's plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, but you meant because this was what the international community required.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At Butmir airport. The Serb side was maximalist, if I can put it that way. They wanted more. 70 per cent was not enough of the territory that they had occupied. It sought for more territory in Herzegovina, right up to the Neretva River and down further to Metkovici and up northwards towards Sarajevo until up to Jablanica, but right up to the Neretva River, in general terms. Of course, the Croatian side, us Croats, we followed their conduct and behaviour. We wanted to obtain the maximum amount of territory possible and wanted the Croatian area to extend until Stolac, which is where the hills are. And there need not be any conflict over those deserted areas there. And of course, the other parts, Konjic, central Bosnia, et cetera. However, they remained adamant in their demands, and we remained adamant too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: May I ask you when the meeting ended.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting ended at around 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you put anything to paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing was written down. We decided not to publish anything, not to publish any information from our discussion, because we had reached no agreement. Each side remained adamant and stood by its original positions. The Croatian delegation left by car to Zagreb, and the Serb delegation took the plane back and went off in an unknown direction. I don't know where they went to. But the whole of the Croatian delegation spent the night at the Intercontinental Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Intercontinental Hotel in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You must be aware of the fact that the Judges are not aware and cannot follow you the way I can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used my official car. It was a Volkswagen Golf. And we returned to Mostar, that is to say to Herzegovina, after having breakfast, having spent the night there. So we were fulfilled the task we were set at Butmir airport in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the usher please and the registrar to provide P126.1 document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat the number of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm going to show you this document, although it is in English. It is the alleged agreement which the delegation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. [Interpretation] P126.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The next page. It is in English. I know you don't speak English.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I can say in conclusion that up until that moment, up until we parted ways, there was no written record or minutes of the meeting, no written record. Later on, a month or two later, I heard that the Serb side had issued a communique of some kind. But I consider, as did the Muslims -- as the Muslim side did too, they gave this communique and report with the aim of separating the Croatian side from the Muslim side, forming a rift, saying that we had had secret negotiations with the Serbs, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was it in fact secret? Did you inform Mr. Izetbegovic about the meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't secret. How could we meet in secret at the airport building in Graz, Austria with the presence of journalists? As soon as we left the premises, the room we were in, some ten journalists surrounded us, bombarding us with questions, asking us to make a statement. But we were in a hurry, and we just went off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can we therefore conclude that there was no agreement, written or signed, of any kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No agreement, no contract, no document of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, following Cutilheiro's request, did you have a second meeting with the Muslims to discuss the same topic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We held our talks in Split, whereas we should have met on the 17th in Split. But three days before that, we were to have met in Prozor. However, Alija Izetbegovic and Ganic and I think Silajdzic - at least that's what we were told - were not able to reach the place with the UNPROFOR transporter because -- APC, because the Croatian delegation had reached Prozor, but they were not able to get there. So that then we had a telephone conversation and decided to meet in Split, which we in fact did on the 17th of May, 1992 to discuss the same issue. However, Alija did not turn up. Ganic didn't turn up either. They had sent a second-rate delegation, second rate in terms of importance with respect to the SDA party leadership. So it was a second-rate delegation in the form of Mr. Tonkovic, the president of the SDA; Ilija Sabic, also from Zagreb. So there was Tonkovic, there was Sabic -- and Tonkovic from Zagreb; and Alija Hodzic, who was the director of a bank in Zenica. And on our part, from our side, there was myself; once again Mr. Milenko Brkic, the acting president of the SDS in Bosnia-Herzegovina; and Palameta, a professor -- a distinguished professor and member of the SDS, Croatian Democratic Union. And the same topic, the same issue, was discussed. Actually, three options were put on the table. Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state was one, in a confederation with the Republic of Croatian. That's the first. The second option would be as follows: Bosnia-Herzegovina as a federally organised state within Bosnia-Herzegovina with three nations, three constituent units. Or the third option, which would be the one advocated by the Muslims, which was a unitarian Bosnia-Herzegovina without any decentralisation, according to canton, federal units, and so on and so forth. And the opinion prevailed as follows: Let's try and agree that this should be -- that the state should be called Bosnia-Herzegovina, a decentralised one internally but with -- and in a confederation with the Republic of -- forming a confederation with the Republic of Croatia. On the occasion, and in view of the fact that these were just talks that were held, we decided not to publicise our talks and not to make them public. But as soon as Mr. Tonkovic and Mr. Sabic arrived back in Zagreb, they told journalists straight away that the Croats and the Muslims had in fact reached an agreement as to how the future system and organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were there any other attempts that you know of or agreements signed at that time along those lines, such as the Tudjman/Izetbegovic agreement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was, in my view, a very significant agreement between Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. Alija signed the meeting as president of the Presidency, that's true, of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Tudjman as President of the Republic of Croatia. In that agreement, a lot was written down. As far as I remember, the agreement, for the first time, was one in which Alija Izetbegovic mentioned the HVO. The HVO was mentioned for the first time. And he said that the HVO should have a united organisation of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina vis-a-vis the Serb side, especially as opposed to the JNA, and to set up ambassadorial relationships. Dual nationality, dual citizenship was recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You mean dual citizenship?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, dual citizenship for Croats in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What about the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You mean for the citizens?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that dual citizenship was recognised. Furthermore, should the international community continue to act as passively as it had been doing towards Bosnia-Herzegovina and allowing the JNA to take over, then Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina would have to undertake other measures, stronger steps, and perhaps cooperate with some other states in order to resist further onslaughts and the liberation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was a military agreement on cooperation signed between the republics?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Military agreement, military cooperation, yes, because the HVO was recognised officially. On the 10th and 11th of April it was rejected by Alija, but in this new agreement he said that he accepted and recognised the HVO as a force on a footing of equality with the army. I think it had already been formed. The TO had grown to become the BH army, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Croatian army could legally, in cooperation with the HVO in Bosnia-Herzegovina, act in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of that agreement, it was understood that Croatia could stand up in defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and oppose the Serb side. That is to say that it could assist both the HVO and the BH army to set up a joint resistance to the further takeover of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I was going to show you a copy of the agreement, but I don't think we need lose time over that because you've explained it to us already. Tell us, please: The agreement that we're talking about, what date was that? What was happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was signed on the 21st of July, 1992. However, I was out in the field, and pursuant to a presidency decision, I was in charge of -- I was set the task of looking after Herzegovina and Central Bosnia. And Ganic was to have gone out into the field as well and to control the area, to tour the area with me and to help the population in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Might I interrupt you? I apologise. But when I asked you, I was thinking about what was going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina up until the 21st of July. What was the war like, the refugees, and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that respect, across the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, into Croatia, and further on to other European countries, over 400.000 Muslims crossed from various parts of Central Bosnia, Northern Bosnia, and especially from Eastern Bosnia. Those who had been expelled and who had been persecuted went to the southern regions, to Dalmacija especially, in Croatia, and other parts of Croatia, and further afield as well, to third countries in Western Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And who looked after those refugees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, who else but the Croatian people in the Croatian Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: All right. And what was the fate of the agreement? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But for the record, please, before we go on to that question, may it be reflected that we are dealing with Exhibit P159.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But to get back to the agreement, what was the fate of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As member of the Presidency, I wanted to check out the political reception that the agreement had got in Bosnia, and Central Bosnia in particular, and I organised three meetings. One was on the 30th of July, in Zenica; the next one was, I think, on the 31st of July of that same year, in Fojnica; and then on the 2nd -- or rather, the 1st of August of that same year, in Jablanica; on the 4th or 5th of August, once again of that same year, in Kakanj; and I organised another one on the 7th of August in the same year, in Zepce. The goal was the same. My object was to see whether Alija Izetbegovic had implemented the agreement among his followers and the inhabitants, the followers and sympathisers of the SDA party, whether it had taken effect at grass-roots level. We discussed the same topics at the meetings. These topics were the political situation in that particular locality; next, cooperation between the HVO and the BH army; then cooperation between the HDZ and the SDA party in the area; and humanitarian aid, because lots of people lived from humanitarian aid in those parts. At each of these meetings we had certain specific local topics to discuss, so that in all the discussions and talks that we had, both the Muslim and the Croat side -- and there were representatives both of the HVO and of the BH army and representatives of the Muslim people and representatives of Croatia in parliament, religious dignitaries from both sides, from both churches and faiths, and so on and so forth. So I tried to rally all these people, and in Jablanica there were over 300 people attending the meeting. I was able to rally all these different profiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did anything else specific happen in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just say that before each of these joint meetings, I would first of all hold a meeting, which might last for an hour, with representatives of the Croatian Community and the HDZ, because I was its candidate, and I found myself a member of the Presidency, thanks to the party. So I would hold a meeting with them first to sound out their opinions and problems. And in Jablanica, the President of the HDZ - his name was Rogic, a man called Rogic - also the other members informed me and asked me, they said, "Mr. Boras, do what you can today. Do your best to ensure that we're not attacked this evening by the armed forces of the army." And I asked them, "What are you talking about?" And they said, "We have received reliable information that they are preparing to attack us." And that was, let's say, before Doljani, six or seven months before Doljani. So at that meeting, as I chaired the meeting -- I chaired the meeting and I did succeed in preventing this from happening on that occasion, but unfortunately it did come to pass at a later date. This meeting in Jablanica was attended by Pasalic, army General Pasalic, who was later to become commander of the 4th Corps in Mostar, and he said on the occasion that there were no problems in Mostar and its environs, no problems with the HVO and the HDZ, that they were cooperating very well and that there were no problems there, whereas Zejnil Delalic - I think he was from Konjic - he attacked the HVO. He did quite the opposite. He attacked the HVO, beginning with Kiseljak and down to Jablanica. He said that they should not be in the area because the army was enough; the BH army was sufficient to guard and protect those regions and that the HVO should disappear from the area. He went as far as saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you ever attend a meeting in Busovaca, for example?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you tell me a date, because I was in Central Bosnia on many occasions, and Busovaca included. So could you give me a date, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes. We have a minutes provided to us by the Prosecution. The date is the 22nd of September, 1992. It is Exhibit P175. The document is Exhibit P175. And the date, as I said, is the 22nd of September, 1992, the meeting in Busovaca, at which you yourself were present. I'm reading that from the minutes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I remember it now. I just happened to come to the meeting by chance, going back from Kakanj, returning from Kakanj, and Kakanj was under the control of the BH army. And in the morning -- I had spent the morning in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I will provide you with a copy of the minutes. I think it is in the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it well. This meeting was held on the 22nd of September, 1992. I think I can see it here, around 1400 hours. Yes, that's right. It was at 1400 hours. At that time I was returning from Kakanj, and Kakanj, as is well known, was under the control -- and the Muslims were in the majority there, and it was under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was involved in talks there with the director of the coal mine and with the defence headquarters, the municipal headquarters, which was headed by the chief of the municipality of Kakanj. And I was involved in talks which concerned the delivery, the supply of electricity from the hydroelectric plant in Kakanj from the -- and before the war, the Republic of Croatia financed about 50 megawatts of electricity from this power plant for the needs of the Croatian republic. During the war, Dalmatia, and in particular Southern Dalmatia, remained without electricity. And in those areas, there were about 200.000 Muslim refugees in the area along the coast itself and on the islands. And I insisted on the fact that the coal mine wasn't working because the power plant wasn't working. The power plant wasn't working because they didn't want to supply Croatia -- the Croatian republic with electricity. So the people from the coal mine asked me to try and influence the municipal leadership and get this situation to change, to ensure that the mine could operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Boras, if we can return to the meeting in Busovaca. You said that you were there quite by accident.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was only listed here. And I informed the members there, those who were present, what I had spoken about in Kakanj. And I was in a hurry to get to Mostar, and I left this meeting. I was just put on the record here, and I told them, you know, what we had spoken about in Kakanj, and I headed on towards Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And did the SDA party support this agreement, and did the HDZ party support this agreement? What were their positions? Was this discussed at the presidency -- was the agreement discussed at the presidency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The presidency never discussed this agreement, although Alija Izetbegovic as the president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina had signed it. As things developed, in my opinion he signed it as the president of the SDA party because the presidency had never discussed this. And the SDA party never agreed to it either. However, to return to the 8th -- that is to say, to the 9th of August, when returning from Central Bosnia on that date, a meeting was held in Prozor, that is to say, in Ramne [phoen]. It was the extended membership of the presidency of the HDZ. And when I was returning, I attended that meeting, and I informed them of what I had spoken about in the Central Bosnia area with regard to the Tudjman/Izetbegovic agreement. And the HDZ presidency, they expressed their full agreement with that -- their full support of that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Just to turn to the initiative of the international community. Did the Security Council of the UN issue certain resolutions? I just want to mention the London Conference, the Geneva Conference, and then the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Cutilheiro's plan and the talks which had to do with Cutilheiro's plan came to a bad conclusion on the 15th of September, 1992. Then the London Conference was held, which -- nothing was solved at this conference either. But they did -- in form of the conversations of the talks about Yugoslavia and the situation in Yugoslavia, within its republics, it took the talks to Geneva. And then at the London Conference, which was chaired by Lord Carrington, right at the very beginning he said that this conference would not solve anything. But with regard to Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were certain particular conclusions. I don't remember them exactly. But I do remember that it was -- the contacts of Bosnia and Herzegovina with other states, with neighbouring states, was made impossible, especially with regard to obtaining weapons. This was done in very explicit terms. And the authority of the UN was extended through UNPROFOR. UNPROFOR was to take up position between the various peoples, to intervene between the various peoples, that is to say, between the Serbian side and the Muslim side and the Croatian side, in order to prevent weapons from arriving. Only humanitarian aid was supposed to arrive and was supposed to be delivered to all those who needed it. So in brief, that would be what I have to say about the London Conference. And then the talks about the internal system in the republics, in particular in Bosnia and Herzegovina, these talks were taken to Geneva. So now we get to the Vance-Owen Plan. I think that started in October 1992, and it was concluded around the -- around March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What was this plan, and who signed it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Vance-Owen Plan, the internal order for Bosnia and Herzegovina was set out, and it was based on the principle of provinces. Ten provinces were to be established. Each people was to have three provinces. And the tenth province was to be Sarajevo, and Sarajevo was to be in a certain sense a free district, a free province. That plan was -- in January, the Croatian side -- in January 1993, the Croatian side signed that plan. There were certain reservations on the part of the Muslim side, as far as I can remember. On the 15th of February, the Muslim side signed with certain reservations. And even under great pressure, the Serbian side -- and I don't think this was until Athens in April or towards the end of April -- the Serbian side signed it. But the Assembly of the Republika Srpska did not support this signature that Karadzic had appended to the agreement, so they -- to the plan, so they held a referendum. They held a referendum. And the Vance-Owen Plan was rejected at this referendum. So that would be the story in brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And then were there any other changes and in the presidency? Could we talk about the constitutional character of the presidency. Or was it a totally illegitimate organ by that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps a little later, not only with regard to the Vance-Owen Plan. It was not until the talks had been held about the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan. Talks on this matter were concluded somewhere around the 20th of August, 1993. And for the first time at these talks -- the War Presidency participated in these talks for the first time. And this was at the request of Lord Owen and Mr. Stoltenberg. They wanted to check to see how the War Presidency regarded this in a unified manner, and they wanted to see how Alija Izetbegovic and the SDA party presented this. And from Zagreb, where we held meetings for about 15 days -- there were suggestions from Zagreb which arrived in the War Presidency. We went to Geneva. But neither Alija Izetbegovic nor Ejub Ganic wanted to go with the other members of the War Presidency. So it was up to me to head the War Presidency. We went to Geneva without Alija Izetbegovic and Ganic. And together with Lord Owen and with Stoltenberg, we discussed these -- these suggestions that they had put forward. And they had suggested a union of three republics within Bosnia-Herzegovina. After about 15 days, we returned home to have a rest, to see our families, and we then returned -- maybe it was towards the end of July 1992. But at that point, Alija Izetbegovic also came. He went to participate in the meetings of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Had his mandate expired by that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His mandate as the president of the presidency expired towards the end of 1992. The first mandate was for one year, and then it could be extended. It was extended in accordance with the rules of the presidency for another year. And that second year it expired towards the end of -- it was the 20th of December, 1992. As soon as Alija Izetbegovic came to the meeting of the War Presidency in Geneva -- just before that first meeting with Alija, we met the members -- the Croatian members of the War Presidency, myself, Akmadzic, Miro Lasic. We met with Tatjana Ljujic-Mijatovic and with Mirko Pejanovic. We met at the Geneva lake. We went for a walk. We were glad to see each other. And I told them, "Tomorrow, we'll ask for the first item on the agenda to be the replacement of Alija Izetbegovic, to have him replaced as the president." His mandate had expired in accordance with the rules. They promised to support us. And thus encouraged, I and my associates from the Croatian delegation, that is to say, the other members, we met in the morning. The agenda was set. Alija didn't mention the possibility of being a replacement then. He was still at the head. And I asked for an extraordinary item -- for the first item on the agenda to be his replacement. There was a vote, and unfortunately Tatjana Ljujic-Mijatovic and Mirko Pejanovic, the Serbian members, did not support us. They did not support our proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Those are the same members who Alija Izetbegovic had brought in of his own free will.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mirko Pejanovic came legally on the basis of that decision adopted by the War Presidency. But Tatjana Ljujic, she came because this is what Alija Izetbegovic wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And when did -- according to what you know, when was Alija Izetbegovic replaced as president of the presidency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he stayed on there, well, almost for life. Even after the Dayton Agreement, he stayed on in the presidency; after 1996, that is to say. And the objective was -- the objective of our arrival in Geneva, the objective of the War Presidency, and the wishes and the objectives of Lord Owen and Mr. Stoltenberg - and this was the objective of the Croatian members, too - the objective was to elevate the War Presidency to a position above those of the delegations of the various peoples so that Alija, who had a dual role -- for one moment he would head the Muslim delegation in talks with the Croatian delegation, and then at other times he would head the Muslim delegation when talks were being held with the Serbian delegation with regard to the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And then when it was necessary, he would also meet with the War Presidency. And the War Presidency, given that people who were suitable in his eyes and who would obey him, this War Presidency would always support Alija Izetbegovic's choices, the option, the option of Alija Izetbegovic. And Lord Owen and Stoltenberg wanted to see whether Alija Izetbegovic had this dual role. And they were persuaded of this. They were persuaded that he was playing a two-faced game, that he had a dual game.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you tell me now something about the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan. What was the nature of this plan and what was agreed on with regard to this plan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, basically, it was a proposal for the union of three republics so that all three peoples should have their own republic within Bosnia and Herzegovina. So Bosnia-Herzegovina, in accordance -- according to this conception, according to this idea, was to be a federal state based on the agreements between these three republics: the Serbian republic, the Muslim republic, and the Croatian republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did Izetbetgovic -- did Mr. Izetbegovic bring any support from those who were in the opposition or from people in Geneva to --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He headed a fairly large delegation. They were not members of the presidency at all. But later on, given that they gave him false legitimacy, he brought in Mijo Stojakovic, a former member of the central committee, and then Ivo Komsic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: A bit slower, please, just for the sake of the transcript, to enter it into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I was saying Nijaz Durakovic, Ivo Komsic, Zulfikar Pasic, Muhamed Filipovic, Kasim Trnka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Is Kasim Trnka the same man who was the President of the Constitutional Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the same time he was the President of the Constitutional Court. And he was with Alija and was helping him with his plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Constitutional Court in September 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we've reached another one of these points where we need more specificity on the circumstances and dates, because I'm not sure, when he talks about the same time as the Constitutional Court, for instance, what time are we talking about? I think despite Mr. Krsnik's desire to go quicker, some of these things have to be taken step by step in some detail, otherwise it's really not helpful to the Chamber or does not assist the -- frankly, the Prosecution in assessing the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with my learned colleague, and I accept his objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Boras, we are talking about very important things for us. So before I asked you about Mr. Trnka, what time are we talking about? What dates are involved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was from the 1st of August, 1993, up until the 20th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And this was all taking place in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was all taking place in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were you living in Geneva at the time, the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were living there in hotels. Some of us, the Croatian members, we weren't being paid, or not completely, by Alija Izetbegovic. Some of it was paid for, the accommodation, but the other funds came from the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But who gave you money for these trips?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, we received money from Alija Izetbegovic. It came out of the treasury of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you a very short question. What changes occurred in the Presidency at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 20th of August, 1993, talks came to an end, talks regarding this plan, regarding the Owen-Stoltenberg plan, so the plan for a union of three republics in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the Croatian members of the War Presidency, given that we had not succeeded in separating the War Presidency from party agreements - and the war was still raging between the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO - given that this was the case, we gave a statement in Geneva for the press and we said that we, the members of the War Presidency - and I have already mentioned the composition - we said that we were ceasing to be members of the War Presidency while there was ongoing fighting between the HVO and the army of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And at that time, did Izetbegovic, did Mr. Izetbegovic assume the Presidency -- did he fill the Presidency with friends of his, in unconstitutional terms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not until after that - I know this about myself - I was dismissed. He dismissed me from the War Presidency. This was in one decision. I was dismissed, and Mr. Lasic too. And I heard a little earlier on before that that Mile Akmadzic had also been dismissed from the War Presidency, and Mr. Abdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And Mr. Abdic, Alija dismissed him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He dismissed him because he was not satisfied with our performance in Geneva and with our request to have him replaced as president.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But it's possible to replace you only at these elections; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the constitution states.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you can't be replaced until there are new elections?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You either have to resign yourself, or it can be a case of death, or the electorate can decide to have you replaced. There are only those three ways of having you removed: resignation, death, or replacement because of the electoral decision. But Alija thought that he had the right to dismiss me as an ordinary functionary, although we had taken the oath together. What was even sadder was that the people who replaced us were the following: Mr. Kljuic, who had resigned previously. He went back to the War Presidency. So according to the rules, your post in the War Presidency could be terminated through resignation, and Kljuic resigned. I don't know for what reason, but he did resign. He tendered his resignation. And instead of him, in an unlawful way, Miro Lasic took his place. How he got there, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kljuic came back, did he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was dismissed and Miro Lasic was dismissed, Kljuic was reinstated. He came back to the Presidency. It had nothing to do with the constitution and laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What about other members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivo Komsic became a member, who had been travelling the world at Alija Izetbegovic's side. He came to replace me. I was dismissed, and then, according to the results of the elections, Ivo Komsic came to take up this post in the Presidency. And instead of Abdic -- and Abdic was replaced by Nijaz Durakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The former president of the Central Committee; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the former president of the Central Committee, who had, throughout the negotiations in Geneva, given support to Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, so Alija had the War Presidency he wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, now, please: I was asking you about Mr. Kasim Trnka. There was an objection a moment ago from the Prosecution, so I wanted to round off that topic. But do you know whether the Constitutional Court at all existed since September 1992? Was it in existence after that date? And do you know - and if so, could you explain to the Trial Chamber - whether it could make any decisions in the composition which the constitution provided for? And I'm talking about the Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, to the best of my knowledge - and it was a situation of war - the War Presidency, under conditions of that kind, takes over all the competencies and authorities of the parliament. The Constitutional Court was left just with the Muslims. The Serbs who were members of the Constitutional Court had left, so had the Croats, and there was no legal logic for them to be able to make any kind of decision. And even if they did make decisions, I didn't know, and I don't know whether they did or didn't, but whatever it was, it was all derogated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Chamber will know that the Prosecution has made very few interruptions during this direct examination, but I think this is an area where he truly is expressing relatively technical opinion. Now, I realise he was a relatively senior member of the government, by his account, but I think some of these things now, we're talking about interpretation of constitutional law and that sort of thing, and I believe -- I object. There's no foundation for this witness to express an opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is a first-hand witness, an eyewitness. He was in Sarajevo at the time. He was a member of the Presidency at the time. He was living in Sarajevo at the time and knows what was going on and is testifying to the things he knows. My question was a clear-cut one: Could the Constitutional Court function, according to the best of his knowledge. And the witness said yes. I wasn't asking him for his opinion or his positions. I just asked him what he knew, as having been present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think you have to give some guidance to the witness to have a very clear and defined answer to your question, because here we just want to hear what the witness saw and did at a particular time. We are not going to hear the opinions and the comments and the perspectives from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. As far as you were able to note, he did not present his views, but he was testifying about the facts that he personally witnessed. My question about the Constitutional Court was whether the witness knew whether the Constitutional Court functioned or not. And his answer was simple. He said: No, it could not, because the members had stepped down and left, and it had no authority. I think that my question was a clear one and that his answer was clear. He knew that the Serb members had left and the Croat members had left, so it was natural.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: He didn't say that at all. He said he didn't know, twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he did say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I've just been reading the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've just been reading the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you may clear it up, and please bear in mind the views expressed by the Prosecution and by this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, do you know whether the Constitutional Court could function, could be functioning in September 1992? Was it operational?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider personally that it could not have been operational because members of the Serb people and members of the Croatian people had left the Constitutional Court at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions in that regard. Tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. May I take a moment to collect my thoughts?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Boras, we are coming to the end, my final questions. Where were you on the 9th of May, 1993? Where were you on that particular day, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That unfortunate date caught me in Mostar. I was in my apartment in Stjepan Radic Street #74. It was a building near the so-called Vranica building. And if I may continue, may be allowed to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, briefly, please. What happened then, as you say you were there personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that date -- that is to say, I was in Mostar all the time and would travel around Bosnia-Herzegovina performing my functions as Presidency member. My family was in the building that I mentioned a moment ago. Two or three months prior to that, I noticed that preparations were being made for war in Mostar, and these were taking place right round my building and the Vranica building. And I found it a little strange, because three or four months prior to that, in the Vranica building, the HVO had been located there. Suddenly the HVO left the building, left the cellars and basement premises, and moved closer to the centre and to the Neretva River. The headquarters of the BH army took its place, arrived, and it was led by Arif Pasalic. And they started fortifying the building, the Vranica building itself and the adjoining buildings or the buildings close by, like my residential block. They started putting sandbags and sniper nests up. And the building that was in between my own building and this other one, the building was -- so there was a building in between the Vranica building and my own apartment block. There was a passageway through which the tenants of number 74, which was my own building, would use. The BH army made a sniper's nest there. Until a couple of days before this 9th of May, 1993, as a Presidency member, they allowed me to enter the building through this passage, through this sniper's nest. They allowed me to pass that way to enter my building. But the other tenants, the other residents, whether they were Muslims, Croats, or Serbs, were not allowed to pass by that way, to take that passageway, but had to take a circuitous route and take a roundabout route to enter the building. On several occasions I stopped to talk to General Pasalic. I asked him what all that meant, what this fortification was. The Vranica building, up until the third floor, facing my building, I noticed, and towards the western part of Mostar as well, had been fortified and reinforced and it was being prepared for combat. And I asked Arif Pasalic what was going on. What were they -- what were all the preparations about? Who are you going to go to war against? And he said, "Well, if the worst comes to the worst, if something were to crop up, we want to be ready for it." Then I went to see the Croatian defence minister, Mr. Stojic, and asked him the same question. I said, "What's going on?" I said, "Mr. Minister, you are the minister of Croatian Defence. The Muslim side is preparing for war, and I find it hard to enter my building, having to pass through all those fortifications. Other people can't even go that way. They have to go round about, take a roundabout route to get into their own apartment building." Bruno Stojic told me that he did not expect any fighting, any combat operations, as far as he knew. But I was in the building there with seven members of my family. A grandchild had just been born to me at the end of January. And this was four months before September -- before May. And I had two other grandchildren. They were 7 and 8 years old. I had my wife, I had my daughter-in-law and my son, and all these family members. And it was the 9th of May, the morning of the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, but can you tell me: Was the sniper's nest right underneath your window? Could you hear them talking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant between the buildings. There was a sniper's nest -- that is to say, I didn't have direct view of it, but there was a bar on the ground floor where the BH army soldiers would go drinking and stay on until the early hours of the mornings. On that particular morning, the 9th of May, somewhere around 3.00 a.m. - I wasn't able to sleep - I thought that something terrible might happen. I heard these soldiers belonging to the BH army saying, "Come on. Let's go. It's time. It's time to talk up our positions." I heard them say that, and I thought: Well, all right. It's probably something that happens every morning. But on the 9th of May, at 5.00 a.m., 5.13 a.m., there was terrible noise from all sides. Shooting started. There was firing at our windows from the Vranica building, which faces the parking lot. And my building and the Vranica building had a joint parking lot, parking space. It was just 60 or 70 -- they were just 60 or 70 metres apart, so that our windows faced each other, faced onto the parking lot. My windows and their windows faced the parking lot. And there was firing at the windows. So not only me and my family and our apartment, but all the tenants of Stjepan Radic Street number 74 spent 36 hours without being able to get up off the floor. The windows were all shattered, bullet-ridden.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Who did the shooting? Who shot at you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we couldn't see, but the bullets were coming from the Vranica building. That was the only place that those bullets could have come from, and that was where the soldiers of the BH army were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And after 36 hours, 36 hours later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thirty-six hours later the fighting stopped, subsided, and we went to take a look out of our windows. The shooting stopped, and when we went up to the windows, we saw that it was no longer the BH army that was there but that they were the HVO soldiers. And from the last entrance to the Vranica building, we saw people with white flags raised. There might have been about 20 to 25 of them, citizens. I noticed on the occasion that Zijo Demirovic was in front of them, the former president of the SDA party for the Bosnia-Herzegovina region. He was standing in front of them. And I was confirmed that this was so by an HVO soldier. Several HVO soldiers, once they had taken over the Vranica building, entered our own building. And he brought in a bag, a nice-looking bag. And as he recognised me and knew that I was a member of the Presidency, he gave me this bag and said, "I have some important documents here that I found in an apartment belonging to Zijo," or whoever. "Do you want to take possession of this bag, Mr. Boras?" And I said, "No. You keep the bag and give it to your superior officer, commanding officer, and he'll know what to do with it."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You said that citizens came out with the flags. Were they citizens or were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all wearing civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I see. They were all wearing civilian clothing. And who led them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was nearby. You could see the people, and I knew Mr. Zijo himself. I had met him several times before the fighting. I met him in the office of the -- of Jovan Topic and Petar Zelenika, together with Orucevic, right before the fighting started, a month before the fighting. They had very close ties. So I would go to visit Topic from time to time. I would stop by and would find them there on several occasions. We even had a cup of coffee together several times and discussed the problems that existed in Mostar and the whole situation there. And I -- not even in my wildest dreams did I ever think that there would be any fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We have to end there for today. It is a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have reached the very Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. end of my examination-in-chief. I come to Medjugorje, the Heliodrome, and half an hour more for my questions, all relating to what the witness saw himself firsthand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Mr. Usher, would you please show the witness out of the room first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: at 1.46 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 28th day of March, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
